reasoning: The package is a standard -bin package that downloads a pinned .deb from the official GitHub releases with verified checksums. The disagreement stems from a false positive where a model assumed that an executable named 'ai.opencode.desktop' was a .desktop metadata file being executed as a binary. In Linux, file extensions do not dictate file type, and this is simply the name chosen by the upstream developers for their binary. There is no malicious injection by the AUR maintainer.
disagreement_analysis: qwen3-235b flagged the desktop entry because the Exec path points to a file ending in '.desktop', incorrectly assuming this meant a metadata file was being executed as a binary to obfuscate malicious code. It failed to recognize that the upstream application's binary is simply named 'ai.opencode.desktop'. deepseek-v4-flash correctly identified it as a standard desktop entry pointing to the upstream binary without raising false alarms.
false_positives: qwen3-235b flagged src/usr/share/applications/ai.opencode.desktop.desktop as malicious obfuscation because the Exec path ends in '.desktop'. This is a false positive based on a misunderstanding of Linux file naming conventions; the upstream binary is just named 'ai.opencode.desktop'.
learnings: Models must not assume that a file ending in '.desktop' referenced in an Exec= field is a desktop metadata file being executed. In Linux, binaries can have any name. The model should recognize upstream binary naming quirks rather than flagging them as obfuscation.

Models should differentiate between upstream application behavior/naming and AUR maintainer injections. A weirdly named binary extracted from a verified upstream .deb is not an injection by the AUR maintainer.
